section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section raises several difficulties regarding the wise son's question, including why he specifies "you" and enumerates the three categories of commandments.
section.t: And it must be understood,
for seemingly,
the above explanation that the wise son's question is specifically about the commandments after the Giving of the Torah,
is only an explanation for that which after he says "which the L-rd our G-d commanded" he adds "you" in order to emphasize that his question is not about the commandments of the Patriarchs,
but rather about the commandments which the L-rd our G-d commanded you after the Giving of the Torah.
But this would seemingly be understood even if he had said in a more inclusive language "which the L-rd our G-d commanded us."
Also, it must be understood [regarding] his saying "what are the testimonies, statutes, and judgments,"
for since his question is about the entirety of the commandments, he should have said "what are the commandments"
(or similar),
and why does he specify testimonies, statutes, and judgments.
And especially since the distinction of the categories of testimonies, statutes, and judgments is in the intention of the commandments
[that the commandments of statutes must be fulfilled because they are a command of the Holy One, blessed be He
(I have decreed a decree),
and the commandments of testimonies and judgments must be fulfilled also because of the reason[18]],
and the question "what are the testimonies, etc." is about the drawing down through the performance of the commandments.
Also, it must be understood that the son's question is about all three categories of commandments
(testimonies, statutes, and judgments)
and in the answer "and He commanded us... to do all the statutes, etc." only statutes are mentioned.
Also, it must be understood,
that the distinction among the three categories of testimonies, statutes, and judgments is[19],
that judgments are the commandments that are obligatory from the aspect of intellect
(like robbery, theft, honoring father and mother),
and testimonies are the commandments that are a sign and remembrance
(like Shabbos, Pesach, Sukkah, and Tefillin),
[for] these commandments,
although the intellect by itself
(were it not for the Torah's command)
would not obligate them
[unlike the commandments of judgments, for even had the Torah not been given, we would learn modesty from a cat and theft from an ant[20]],
nevertheless,
after the Torah commanded them, the intellect agrees to them,
and statutes are the commandments that even after the Torah commanded them have no place in intellect,
and they are only in the manner of "a statute I have enacted, a decree I have decreed[21]."
And based on this, seemingly it should have said judgments, testimonies, and statutes
(in an ascending order)
or statutes, testimonies, and judgments
(in a descending order),
and the order in the verse is testimonies, statutes, and judgments.

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains the precise wording of "you" in the wise son's question, noting that it seemingly resembles the wicked son's exclusion of himself.
section.t: And this will be understood by prefacing what was said by my revered father-in-law, the Rebbe, in his discourse beginning with the word "Zeh"[22]
(which he said on the first Passover after his arrival in the United States to dwell)
regarding the precision that in the wise son's question it is written "you,"
for by this that he says "you"
(and not "us")
he seemingly resembles the wicked son.
And he adds in the discourse,
that although the wise son says "our G-d,"
which includes himself within the community of Israel and accepts upon himself the yoke of the kingdom of heaven,
nevertheless, this is regarding the essential[23],
but regarding the particular details of testimonies, statutes, and judgments,
he says "you."
For from the language of the discourse it implies that the precision in this that he says "you" is not only that it requires explanation why he says "you,"
but also in this that he says "you" and not "us,"
that through this there is room for error that this that he says "our G-d" and includes himself in the collective,
is only regarding the essential
(acceptance of the yoke of the kingdom of heaven),
but regarding the particular details of testimonies, statutes, and judgments he excludes himself from the collective.

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that there are two aspects in the commandments—the general command of G-d and the specific categories—and the wise son's question concerns the relevance of the categories.
section.t: And the explanation of this can be said,
that in the commandments there are two matters.
That the commandments are a command of G-d,
[for] this matter is equal in all the commandments,
and that the commandments are divided into three categories of testimonies, statutes, and judgments.
And these two matters are also in the fulfillment of the commandments.
For in the intention of the commandments,
there are two matters[24].
A general intention – to fulfill the command of G-d,
[for] this intention is equal in all the commandments.
And a particular intention – fulfilling the commandment because it is a testimony
(a sign and remembrance)
regarding some matter,
or because it is a statute and decree[25],
or because it is obligatory also from the aspect of intellect.
And the wise son's question "what are the testimonies, statutes, and judgments" is,
[that] since all the commandments are a command of G-d,
what relevance does the matter of testimonies, statutes, and judgments have.

Therefore it is precise in the discourse that even after he says "our G-d" there is room for error that regarding the particular details of testimonies, statutes, and judgments he excludes himself, G-d forbid, from the collective.
And in order to negate this error, he should have said "us."
